name: Lake Abbe
blurb: A salt lake in the Afar rift where flamingos, gazelles and scavengers share scarce water.

tip.title: Cut the Awash River
tip.text: Almost all of the lake's water arrives via the Awash. Lower it and watch the algae, then the flamingos, and the scavengers that depend on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Intense, nearly year-round sun drives plant growth and also the heat and evaporation that make the basin so dry.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, algae and carcasses where moisture allows, returning nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Spirulina and other cyanobacteria
nodes.desc: Blue-green algae that thrive in very alkaline, salty lakes and are the main food of lesser flamingos. Their presence here is inferred from flamingo use of the lake.
Flat-topped thorny tree of dry wadis and lowlands in Djibouti. Its leaves and pods feed browsers.
Filters spirulina, other algae and tiny invertebrates from alkaline lakes with its deep bill. Flamingos are the wildlife noted at Lake Abbe.
Eats leaves, shoots and seeds of many plants, roughly its body weight daily, and can form huge swarms after rains.
Small gazelle that mostly eats acacia leaves, flowers and pods plus desert bushes. Gets most of its water from succulents.
Pig-like grazer that also digs for roots; recorded in the area and listed as vulnerable in Djibouti.
Eats invertebrates, rodents, reptiles and small mammals up to gazelle fawns, plus carrion and fruit. Recorded eating donkeys here.
Strict carrion feeder that travels over 100 km from its nest and gathers at carcasses with other vultures.
Mainly a scavenger of ungulate carcasses that also kills smaller animals and eats fruit. A natural predator of hamadryas baboons.
